pages.x: As the Mughal Empire crumbled, the Marathas of western India became the strongest power in the land. By 1758 their horsemen had reached Lahore and the river Indus, and the Mughal emperor in Delhi was in their hands.

Ahmad Shah Durrani had founded the kingdom of Afghanistan in 1747, and had already raided India several times, sacking Delhi in 1757. He would not let the Marathas keep the Punjab. In 1759 he came down through the passes again, and Muslim princes of India, the Rohillas and the nawab of Awadh, joined him.

The Marathas sent a great army north under Sadashivrao Bhau, with cannon trained in the French style, and tens of thousands of pilgrims and camp followers came with it. The two armies dug in facing each other near Panipat, north of Delhi, and for two months they waited, while food in the Maratha camp ran out.

On 14 January 1761 the starving Marathas attacked. Their guns tore holes in the Afghan lines, but in the afternoon Durrani threw in his reserves, and the Maratha army broke. Bhau was killed. The next day thousands of prisoners were massacred, and camp followers who could not escape were killed or enslaved.
pages.of: killed in one of history's bloodiest days

pages.x: Durrani's soldiers, unpaid for two years, wanted to go home, and he went back to Afghanistan without taking the Mughal throne. Within ten years the Marathas were strong again in the north. But the battle had weakened both of India's great powers, and the British, gaining ground in Bengal, were the real winners.

Panipat became a byword in India for disaster. It ended the Marathas' hopes of ruling all India, and cleared the way for the British East India Company. In Afghanistan Ahmad Shah is remembered as Ahmad Shah Baba, the father of the nation.
pts: One of the bloodiest days of the century
It opened the way for British rule in India
